question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
answer:
Counterspell resolves first, and no, Divination does not resolve — it gets countered and never has its effect (drawing two cards).

Since Counterspell was cast targeting Divination while Divination was still on the stack, Counterspell was cast "in response to" Divination, which means Counterspell was placed on top of the stack and will resolve before Divination does [117.7]. When all players pass in succession, only the topmost object on the stack resolves [608.1] [405.5] [117.4] — that's Counterspell, not Divination.

When Counterspell resolves, its text ("Counter target spell") checks that Divination is still a legal target [608.2b], then executes: Divination is countered, meaning it is canceled and removed from the stack — it does not resolve and none of its effects (drawing two cards) occur. The countered Divination is put into its owner's graveyard [701.6a]. Note also that the caster of Divination gets no refund of the mana spent to cast it [701.6b].

After Counterspell finishes resolving (is removed from the stack per [608.2n]), players will receive priority again, but there is nothing left on the stack representing Divination — it's already gone to the graveyard, so it will never get a chance to resolve.

question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
answer:
You need assign 3 combat damage to Vampire Nighthawk before then's toughness of3, then then Charging Rhino's damage assignment) before any leftover trample damage over to the defending player, since since Charging Rhino itnot deathtouch, so normal lethal-damage rules apply rather than than the deathtouch rule.

According ability [702.19b], for an attacking creature with trample the controller must assign at least lethal damage to each blocking creature before assigning any damage to the player/planeswalker/battle it's attacking. "Lethal damage" for a creature is damage greater than or equal to its toughness, taking into account damage already marked on it and damage from other sources being assigned in the same combat damage step [702.19b], [120.6], [704.5g].

Vampire Nighthawk has toughness 3 and no damage currently marked on it, so lethal damage for it is 3. Deathtouch would only lower the lethal-damage threshold to 1 if the *source dealing the damage* had deathtouch (per [702.2c] and [120.4a]) — but that deathtouch belongs to Vampire Nighthawk, not to Charging Rhino, the attacker doing the assigning. Charging Rhino's own card text gives it no deathtouch, and nothing in the question suggests it gained deathtouch, so the deathtouch on Vampire Nighthawk is irrelevant to how Charging Rhino assigns its damage.

So: assign exactly 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk (its toughness) to satisfy the lethal-damage requirement, then you may assign all of Charging Rhino's remaining power as trample damage to the defending player. Since Charging Rhino is a 4/4, that leaves 1 damage that can trample through to the player.

Note: if Vampire Nighthawk already had damage marked on it before this combat damage assignment, you'd only need to assign enough additional damage to reach its toughness of 3 total, per [120.6] and [702.19b]'s instruction to account for damage already marked.

question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
answer:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers before the cascaded spell resolves. Here's why: when Shardless Agent's cascade ability resolves, you cast the exiled nonland spell as part of resolving that ability. Casting a spell is itself an event that can cause triggered abilities to trigger [601.2i], and if that cascaded spell is noncreature, it satisfies prowess's trigger condition ("Whenever you cast a noncreature spell...") [702.108a]. Per Monastery Swiftspear's own rulings, prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger, and resolves before that spell [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2], and this is true even if the triggering spell is later countered [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #3]. Shardless Agent's own ruling confirms this pattern for cascade: casting the exiled spell puts it on the stack above the spell with cascade [Shardless Agent ruling #1], and any prowess-style triggers from that casting would similarly stack on top of it. So the timeline is: Shardless Agent is cast (as an Artifact Creature, this does NOT trigger Monastery Swiftspear's prowess, since Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1 says spells with the creature type never trigger prowess) → Shardless Agent's cascade ability triggers and is put on the stack above Shardless Agent [603.1] → cascade resolves, exiling cards and letting you cast the exiled nonland, noncreature card → that casting triggers prowess, which is put on the stack on top of the newly cast spell → prowess resolves, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 until end of turn, and only then does the cascaded spell itself resolve. This holds regardless of whether you're in a two-player or multiplayer game, since it depends only on stack/trigger mechanics, not on turn order or priority among opponents.

question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
answer:
Yes — but not because of Lightning Bolt. Grizzly Bears is a 2/2, so 2 damage marked on it is already lethal (damage marked ≥ toughness). Once that damage is marked, the very next time state-based actions are checked, Grizzly Bears will be destroyed [120.6][302.7]. State-based actions are checked and applied every time a player would receive priority, and this happens automatically without anyone getting priority in between [704.1][704.2][117.5][405.6f][117.2d]. That means Grizzly Bears would be destroyed as a state-based action before you'd even get priority to cast Lightning Bolt in the first place — the damage was already lethal before the Bolt entered the picture. So if you're asking whether Grizzly Bears dies from its existing 2 damage before your Lightning Bolt resolves, the answer is yes, and in fact it would already be dead before the spell was cast/targeted at all (assuming the 2 damage was marked before you cast Lightning Bolt). Note that even if Lightning Bolt's 3 damage is what pushes it over (i.e., you're really asking about the combined 2+3=5 damage once Lightning Bolt resolves), the destruction still happens via a state-based action after the damage is dealt, not from the damage or the spell directly — rule 120.5 makes clear that neither Lightning Bolt nor its damage destroys the creature; state-based actions do that once damage marked (2, or 2+3=5) is greater than or equal to toughness 2. If instead the 2 damage was marked simultaneously with or after Lightning Bolt's resolution (an unusual ordering), the SBA check still happens right after that damage is applied and before either player gets priority again, so Grizzly Bears would die immediately after, not 'before,' Lightning Bolt resolves — I'm assuming the more natural reading that the 2 damage was already on Grizzly Bears prior to casting/resolving Lightning Bolt.

question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
answer:
Both triggered abilities trigger at the same moment: the instant your upkeep step begins (rule 500.6, 603.2b). Since the upkeep step has no turn-based actions (503.1a, 703.3), there's nothing to resolve automatically first — the triggers go straight onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority (500.6, 603.3b).

No single player "chooses the order" of both triggers as a pair. Instead, each player only orders the triggered abilities *they themselves control*, and APNAP order (101.4) determines who places abilities on the stack first: since it's your upkeep, you are the active player, so you put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first, and then your opponent (the nonactive player) puts their beginning-of-upkeep trigger on the stack second (603.3b, citing 101.4). Because the stack resolves last-on-top, your opponent's trigger will actually resolve *before* your Phyrexian Arena trigger, even though you placed yours on the stack first.

Once both triggers are on the stack, the active player (you) receives priority (503.1a, 117.3a), and players can respond with instants/abilities before anything resolves.

One note on the scenario itself: for your opponent's ability to trigger during *your* upkeep at all, it must be worded to trigger on upkeeps generally (e.g., "at the beginning of each upkeep" or "at the beginning of each player's upkeep"), not just "your upkeep," since a beginning-of-upkeep ability only triggers when the relevant player's own upkeep begins. This answer assumes exactly two players; in a multiplayer game, if more than one nonactive player has such a trigger, they would each add their abilities to the stack in turn order after the active player, per 101.4.

question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
answer:
Only one copy of the card ends up in your hand — the original sorcery card itself, returned by its own buyback ability. The copy created by Fork is not a card at all, so even though its buyback cost was 'paid' as part of the copy inheriting the original spell's payment, there is no physical card for it to put into your hand.

Here's why: when you cast the sorcery and pay its buyback cost, buyback is a static ability meaning 'If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner's hand instead of into that player's graveyard as it resolves' [702.27a]. That works because there's an actual card object to move to your hand.

When you cast Fork targeting that sorcery, resolving Fork puts a copy of the spell onto the stack — this copy 'copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including... additional or alternative costs' [707.10], so the copy is treated as having had its buyback cost paid too. But 'a copy of a spell isn't cast' [707.10], and critically, per Fork's own ruling, 'The copy that is placed on the stack is not considered to have been "cast"' [Fork ruling #9], and 'The Fork card goes to the graveyard when it resolves and leaves the copy on the stack. There is no card representing the copy on the stack' [Fork ruling #10]. Fork's ruling states directly: 'If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you' [Fork ruling #8].

So when the copy resolves, its buyback 'ability' has nothing to send to your hand (there's no card), and when the original sorcery resolves, it returns to your hand as a card because you paid its buyback cost. Net result: 1 card in your hand, not 2.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming you cast the sorcery first, then cast Fork targeting it while the sorcery is still on the stack, so Fork resolves first (putting the copy on top of the stack), the copy resolves next (doing its effect, no card returned), and finally the original sorcery resolves and returns to your hand via buyback. This order doesn't change the final card count either way, since Fork's copy never yields a card regardless of when it resolves relative to the original.

This answer holds the same whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since nothing about buyback, Fork, or copying spells depends on the number of players.

question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
answer:
No token is created. Mimic Vat's activated ability lets you "Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact," but per Mimic Vat's own ruling, if the card exiled is a nonpermanent card — such as an instant or sorcery card that died while manifested (face-down) — you can't create a token copy of it, so no token results. Lightning Bolt is an instant card, so once its manifested permanent died and it was imprinted (exiled) onto Mimic Vat via the imprint ability, the exiled object is a nonpermanent card. When you later activate Mimic Vat's second ability, {3}, {T}: "Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact. It gains haste. Exile it at the beginning of the next end step," the effect tries to make a token copy of that Lightning Bolt card, but tokens copying nonpermanent cards can't be created — this mirrors the general rule that a token copy of a nonexistent or invalid object simply isn't created. This is confirmed directly by Mimic Vat's own ruling: if the creature that died was an instant or sorcery card that had been manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled, and you can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card, so no token is created in that case. You still spend the {3} and tap Mimic Vat, but nothing is created as a result. This holds the same whether you're playing with two players or more, since nothing about Mimic Vat's ability depends on player count.

question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
answer:
Yes — both exiled creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield exile ability and its leaves-the-battlefield return ability are a linked pair: the return ability's "the exiled card" refers only to cards exiled by that specific exile ability [406.6][607.2a]. Per the Lithoform Engine ruling, if an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability created by Lithoform Engine remain linked to that same second ability [Lithoform Engine ruling #4]. So when you copy Fiend Hunter's exile trigger with Lithoform Engine and choose a new target, the copy is still linked to Fiend Hunter's "return the exiled card" ability, and now two creatures have been exiled by that linked pair (the original trigger and its copy). Since the return ability refers to a single object as "the exiled card" but the linked exile ability (with its copy) has exiled multiple cards, the return ability refers to each of them, and its "perform any actions on 'the' card" instruction is carried out on each exiled card [607.3]. Therefore both creatures return under their owners' control when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield.

question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
answer:
No, the creature stays exiled. Phasing out is not the same as leaving the battlefield: rule [702.26d] states that phasing doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones, and Banishing Light's ability only returns the exiled creature "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." Since Banishing Light merely phases out (and will later phase in) rather than leaving the battlefield, that leave-the-battlefield condition is never met, so the delayed exile effect keeps the opponent's creature exiled.

This is confirmed directly by [Teferi's Protection ruling #21]: "Any one-shot effects that are waiting 'until [this] leaves the battlefield,' such as that of Banishing Light, won't happen when a permanent phases out." Additionally, [Teferi's Protection ruling #17] notes phasing out doesn't trigger any leaves-the-battlefield abilities.

Banishing Light will phase back in under your control at the beginning of your next untap step, per the turn-based action in [502.1] (all your permanents that phased out phase in simultaneously as you untap), consistent with the general phasing rule [610.4]. When it phases in, it's the same permanent that never actually left the battlefield, so its exile effect on the opponent's creature continues uninterrupted.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
answer:
Yes, Counterspell can legally target Emrakul, the Promised End while it's still a spell on the stack, and even if Emrakul is countered, you still gain control of the targeted opponent during their next turn.

Here's why: Emrakul's protection from instants is a static ability of the permanent, and protection abilities (like all abilities of a permanent other than a few stack-only exceptions) function only while that permanent is on the battlefield [113.6g]. While Emrakul, the Promised End is still on the stack as a spell, it has no protection at all — this is explicitly confirmed by [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2], which notes Emrakul may be targeted by a spell like Syncopate (or here, Counterspell) while it's on the stack. So your opponent's Counterspell can target the Emrakul, the Promised End spell without any issue from protection from instants.

As for the trigger: "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn" is a triggered ability that triggers on the event of casting Emrakul, the Promised End, not on it resolving. That means the moment you finish casting Emrakul, the Promised End, this triggered ability is put on the stack as its own separate object, on top of the Emrakul, the Promised End spell [603.1a]. Your opponent's Counterspell, which reads "Counter target spell," can only target and counter the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself — it cannot target or counter the triggered ability, since activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells and can't be countered by anything that counters only spells [113.9].

So the sequence resolves as: Counterspell resolves first (assuming it's cast in response and no one else responds), sending the Emrakul, the Promised End spell to your graveyard uncast/countered. The triggered ability granting you control of your opponent's next turn is still sitting on the stack underneath where Counterspell was, and it resolves normally afterward, unaffected by the spell being countered. You still gain control of the opponent during their next turn, and after that turn, the extra-turn trigger from Emrakul's ability still applies as normal — you just don't get the 13/13 flying, trampling, protection-from-instants body, since the creature itself was countered.

One timing note: this assumes the trigger ability was already placed on the stack before Counterspell was cast (i.e., your opponent is responding to the trigger, as you describe, not somehow countering it before it exists). That matches your description of "in response to its cast trigger," so no ambiguity here changes the outcome.

question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
answer:
Yes, hitting Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a legal cascade trigger, and yes you can attempt to cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free — but whether the free cast actually goes through depends on your cascade spell's own mana value, because Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor's mana value for this purpose is 7, not 2.

Here's why. Cascade [702.85a] says: exile cards from the top of your library until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value, then you may cast that card for free if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card sitting in exile, not on the stack — a card's default state (front face up) applies when it isn't being cast or hasn't entered the battlefield, the same pattern rule 712.11c and rule 712.14b describe for casting and for entering the battlefield. So while it's sitting in exile as an uncast card, its mana value is that of its front face, Valki, God of Lies, i.e. 2. As long as your cascade spell's mana value is greater than 2 (which is true for essentially any cascade spell), exiling into Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a legal, valid cascade hit that stops the exile process.

Now, when you get the option to cast 'that card' for free, [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16] confirms that when an effect lets you cast a card from a group (which is exactly what cascade's follow-up permission does), you may cast a modal double-faced card using either face that fits the effect's criteria — so choosing to cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face is allowed, and [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14] confirms you only check Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor's own characteristics (planeswalker, {5}{B}{R}) for legality, ignoring the Valki, God of Lies side.

The catch is the second mana-value check: 'if the resulting spell's mana value is less than this spell's mana value.' Rules 712.8c and 712.8e explicitly say that the front-face-based mana value calculation (i.e., 'even on the back face, use the front face's mana cost for mana value') applies only to *nonmodal* double-faced cards. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a *modal* double-faced card, so that exception doesn't apply to it — the resulting Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor spell's mana value is simply its own mana cost, {5}{B}{R}, mana value 7. So you can only actually cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for free via this cascade trigger if your cascade spell's mana value is greater than 7; otherwise the cascade ability's free-cast condition fails and Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (along with any other exiled-but-uncast cards) goes to the bottom of your library instead, per cascade's cleanup instruction. You could still cast the front face, Valki, God of Lies (mana value 2), for free from essentially any cascade spell, since 2 is less than almost any cascade spell's mana value.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
You end up controlling only 1 of your opponent's turns, but you do get a second Emrakul, the Promised End, and copying the spell does NOT give you another control‑a‑turn trigger.

Walking through it: When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its triggered ability ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.") goes on the stack above the Emrakul, the Promised End spell. You copy that triggered ability with Lithoform Engine's first activated ability, which puts a copy of the trigger on the stack (per 707.10, a copy of a triggered ability is itself an ability with the same source and decisions, including target). After untapping Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key, you use Lithoform Engine's third ability to copy the still‑on‑the‑stack Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell.

Resolution order (last on, first off): the copy of the Emrakul, the Promised End spell resolves first. Per rule 111.13, "A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves," so you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End on the battlefield as a token copy — yes, you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End. Crucially, this token is not "cast" (707.10, and Lithoform Engine ruling #6: "Creating the copy won't cause abilities that trigger when a player casts a spell... to trigger"), so the "When you cast this spell" trigger does NOT fire again. Copying the spell gives you no additional control-a-turn trigger.

Next, the copied triggered ability resolves, and then the original triggered ability resolves, each independently saying "you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn... after that turn, that player takes an extra turn," both targeting the same opponent's same upcoming next turn. Per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14, "Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works," but "each ability's effect will create an extra turn." Since the two control effects target the very same turn, they overwrite one another — only the last-created one (from the original trigger, which resolves after its copy) actually gives you control of that turn. So you control exactly 1 of your opponent's turns, not 2. However, each resolution still spawns its own delayed extra-turn trigger, so your opponent ends up with two stacked extra turns afterward (added one at a time per rule 500.7, with the most recently created taken first) — that's a side effect worth knowing even though it wasn't the main question.

Assumption: this analysis assumes a single opponent (two-player game) and that you didn't choose a different new target for the Lithoform Engine copy of the trigger. If you're in a multiplayer game and choose a different opponent as the new target for the copied trigger, the overwrite rule wouldn't apply (different players' turns don't overwrite each other), and you'd control one turn from each of two different opponents instead of just one turn total.

question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
answer:
Yes — you end up with two token creatures, not one. When you activate Mimic Vat's ability "Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact...", that activated ability goes on the stack. Lithoform Engine's first ability, "Copy target activated or triggered ability you control," targets that ability and puts a copy of it onto the stack above the original [707.10b]; per Lithoform Engine's own ruling, this creates another instance of the ability on the stack rather than granting anyone an ability [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. A copied ability has the same source as the original ability [707.10b], and since Mimic Vat's ability refers to "this artifact" (i.e., Mimic Vat itself by name/reference), both the original and the copy point to the same Mimic Vat and the same exiled card [201.5a, 707.10b].

Because the copy is created while the original is still on the stack, it resolves first (LIFO), creating a token copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat, giving that token haste, and setting up its exile at the beginning of the next end step, exactly per Mimic Vat's rules text. The original ability then resolves and does the same thing again, creating a second token copy of that same exiled card (assuming the same card is still exiled with Mimic Vat when each ability resolves — see Mimic Vat's own ruling that the token is a copy of whatever is exiled *at the time the ability resolves* [Mimic Vat ruling #4]). Each instance is a completely separate resolution, so you get two hasty token copies, each independently exiled at the beginning of the next end step.

This assumes a normal game state where nothing swaps out the exiled card between the two resolutions and you're not resolving this during a turn's actual end step (which would push the exile timing to the following turn's end step instead, per Mimic Vat's own ruling) — if the exiled card changed between the two resolutions, the two tokens could copy different cards, but you'd still get two tokens either way.

Gutter Grime has an ability that reads “Whenever a nontoken creature you control dies, put a slime counter on this enchantment, then create a green Ooze creature token with ‘This token’s power and toughness are each equal to the number of slime counters on Gutter Grime.’” The ability granted to the token only looks at the Gutter Grime that created the token, not at any other Gutter Grime on the battlefield. A copy of that token would also have an ability that referred only to the Gutter Grime that created the original token.

question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, it still ends up costing {1}{G}{G} (three mana total) and creates zero Forest Dryad tokens — a total waste of the extra mana. The correct choice is X=2: it costs exactly the same {1}{G}{G} (three mana) but nets you two Forest Dryad tokens instead of none.

Here's why. Per rule 107.3a, you choose and announce the value of X for Awaken the Woods as part of casting it, before costs are finalized. Per rule 601.2f (Total Cost), the total cost is built by taking the spell's mana cost with X substituted, then applying additional costs/increases and cost reductions, and only then locking it in.

Awaken the Woods' printed cost is {X}{G}{G}. Your permanent that reduces your green spells by {1} only reduces the generic portion of the cost, and generic mana can't be reduced below {0} (rule 601.2f). So:
- X=0: base cost {G}{G} (0 generic to reduce) → after your reducer, still {G}{G} = 2 total mana.
- X=1: base cost {1}{G}{G} → reducer removes the {1} → {G}{G} = 2 total mana.
- X=2: base cost {2}{G}{G} → reducer removes {1} → {1}{G}{G} = 3 total mana.
- X=3: base cost {3}{G}{G} → reducer removes {1} → {2}{G}{G} = 4 total mana.

Trinisphere then applies as the final step in locking in the total cost (Trinisphere ruling #0): 'each spell that would cost less than three mana to cast costs three mana to cast,' with the extra generic mana payable in any color or colorless. For X=0 and X=1, your cost before Trinisphere is only 2 mana ({G}{G}), which is less than three, so Trinisphere bumps it up to three mana by adding one generic: {1}{G}{G}. For X=2, your cost before Trinisphere is already {1}{G}{G} (3 mana), which is not less than three, so Trinisphere doesn't add anything — it stays {1}{G}{G}. For X=3 it's {2}{G}{G} (4 mana), also untouched by Trinisphere.

So X=0 and X=1 both cost {1}{G}{G} (3 mana) due to Trinisphere's minimum, but give you 0 or 1 token respectively — strictly worse than X=2, which costs the identical {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total: {1} generic, {G}, {G}) but gives you 2 Forest Dryad land creature tokens. Note per rule 202.3e and the Trinisphere ruling, the spell's mana value is based on the X you chose (so mana value 2 at X=0, mana value 4 at X=2, etc.) and is unaffected by how much you actually pay.

If you're willing to spend one more mana, X=3 costs {2}{G}{G} (4 mana) for 3 tokens, which is also efficient (no wasted Trinisphere tax) — but the cheapest 'no waste' point is X=2 at 3 total mana.

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes, you can enchant Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead while it's in your graveyard, but the whole play backfires: Grist comes back, then you're immediately forced to sacrifice it, and Animate Dead ends up in your graveyard too.

Here's why. Animate Dead's enchant ability is "enchant creature card in a graveyard" (per its printed text). Per [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], Grist's own text — "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types" — makes it a Legendary Planeswalker Creature while sitting in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead there.

When Animate Dead resolves and its triggered ability fires, it returns Grist to the battlefield under your control and attaches itself to it ([Animate Dead ruling #1]). But the instant Grist hits the battlefield, its own text stops applying (it's only a creature "as long as Grist isn't on the battlefield"), so Grist becomes just a planeswalker, no longer a creature. Animate Dead's enchant ability requires it to be attached to a creature that was put onto the battlefield by it, and Grist no longer qualifies. This is the same situation described in [Animate Dead ruling #4] for a creature with protection from black or one that otherwise can't legally be enchanted: Animate Dead can't attach, so as a state-based action it gets put into your graveyard, which triggers its delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it"). When that delayed trigger resolves, since Grist (now a planeswalker) is still on the battlefield, you must sacrifice it.

Net result: Grist briefly returns to the battlefield as a planeswalker with 3 loyalty, then you're forced to sacrifice it right away via Animate Dead's leaves-the-battlefield trigger, and Animate Dead itself is already in your graveyard. You don't get to keep or meaningfully use Grist this way — it's essentially a wasted Animate Dead cast unless you have some other way to protect or use the brief window Grist is on the battlefield (e.g., activating a loyalty ability with priority before the sacrifice trigger resolves, since the delayed trigger has to go on the stack and resolve).

Timing note: this assumes Animate Dead resolves normally and its triggered ability returns Grist in the same window described above; there's no ambiguity here since the rulings spell out the sequence explicitly.

question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
answer:
Yes, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters the whole way through, and no, Doubling Season does not double them when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters the battlefield.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own printed text overrides the normal counter-loss rule: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Normally, per rule [122.2] and the zone-change rule [400.7], counters cease to exist whenever an object changes zones, because the new object has no memory of its previous existence. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's text is a specific exception to that general rule.

Tracing the zone changes: when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies, it moves from the battlefield to the graveyard — not hand or library, so its four counters remain. As your commander, you may then move it from the graveyard to the command zone as the state-based action described in rule [903.9a] — again not hand or library, so the counters remain (as confirmed by [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3], which notes a Skullbriar sitting in the command zone with a counter on it has boosted power/toughness even off the battlefield). When you recast it, it moves from the command zone to the stack and then resolves onto the battlefield — neither of those is hand or library either, so the four counters remain on it the whole time, including as it re-enters the battlefield.

Because those counters are retained rather than newly placed, Doubling Season's doubling effect doesn't apply to them. Doubling Season only doubles counters that "would be put" on a permanent you control as a game effect; [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] explicitly states "The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones aren't 'placed' on Skullbriar. Effects like Doubling Season's ... won't affect those counters." So Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters the battlefield as a 5/5 (1/1 base plus four +1/+1 counters), not an 8/8.

Note: this all assumes you're using the normal commander-to-command-zone option in rule [903.9a] rather than some other replacement effect; if a different effect intercepted one of those zone changes and sent Skullbriar, the Walking Grave to your hand or library at any point, the counters would have ceased to exist at that moment per Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text, and it would re-enter with zero counters (which Doubling Season also couldn't help with, since no counters would be placed by that path).

question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
answer:
No — you do not lose the game. Final Fortune's trigger is worded "At the beginning of that turn's end step, you lose the game." If you activate Sundial of the Infinite's ability ("{1}, {T}: End the turn. Activate only during your turn.") before the end step of that extra turn begins, the current phase/step ends immediately and the game skips straight to the cleanup step — the end step itself is skipped entirely and never begins [724.1d]. Because "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities don't trigger when the end step is skipped [724.1e], and this is explicitly confirmed for Sundial of the Infinite (activating it before the end step means those triggers simply never happen that turn, instead waiting for the next turn's end step) [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1], Final Fortune's lose-the-game trigger never fires. Sundial of the Infinite's resolution order also confirms the sequence: the stack is exiled, creatures are removed from combat, state-based actions are checked, and then the current step ends and the game proceeds straight to cleanup — with no priority and no new triggered abilities going on the stack [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4]. Since Final Fortune's trigger condition (the beginning of that turn's end step) never occurs on the extra turn, you survive without losing. This is analogous to the ruling that if the extra turn itself is skipped you don't lose [Final Fortune ruling #1] — here the relevant step within that turn is skipped instead, with the same practical result. If Final Fortune's trigger had already gone on the stack before you activated Sundial of the Infinite, that would be a different situation, but as described you're ending the turn before the end step even begins, so the trigger is never created.

question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
answer:
You choose what Clone copies at the moment Clone enters the battlefield — not earlier during casting — and your opponents get no window to respond to that specific choice.

Clone (Creature — Shapeshifter, {3}{U}, 0/0) reads "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield." Clone's ability doesn't target the chosen creature [Clone ruling #0], so the choice isn't announced as part of the normal targeting steps of casting a spell (rule 601.2c governs target announcement, but that doesn't apply here). Instead, this is a replacement effect that modifies how Clone enters the battlefield: rule [707.5] says an object that enters the battlefield 'as a copy' of another object becomes a copy as it enters — it doesn't enter first and then become a copy. So the copy choice is made right as the Clone spell resolves and Clone is about to enter the battlefield, as part of applying that replacement effect.

Under [707.6], since any 'as this enters' choices aren't preserved from the copied permanent, it's Clone's controller (you) who makes the choice of what to copy, and you also get to make any new 'as [this] enters' choices the copied creature's text calls for (e.g., choosing a creature type if you copy something like Adaptive Automaton). If for some reason multiple replacement effects were competing over how Clone enters the battlefield, [616.1c] would have you (as the affected permanent's controller) pick which one to apply, and if more than one player faced such a choice simultaneously it would be resolved in APNAP order per rule [101.4] — but note the rules given only frame priority/turn order for the two-player case explicitly; in a multiplayer game the same APNAP procedure applies (active player first, then remaining players in turn order), it just involves more players making choices in sequence before the simultaneous action happens.

Because this choice is made as part of a replacement effect during resolution — not by putting something on the stack or announcing a target — there's no priority window where an opponent can respond to it. Your opponents can respond to the Clone spell itself before it resolves (e.g., countering it), and they get priority normally once Clone is on the battlefield as its copy, but they cannot interrupt or respond to the act of choosing what Clone copies.

You may also choose not to copy anything, in which case Clone simply enters as a 0/0 Shapeshifter (and will likely die immediately from having 0 toughness) [Clone ruling #5]. Also, you can only choose a creature that's already on the battlefield — if another creature is entering at the same time as Clone, you can't copy it [Clone ruling #2].

question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
answer:
You get 3 lands total from that single Flooded Strand activation: the original resolution of its ability plus the 2 copies Gogo, Master of Mimicry creates.

Here's why: Flooded Strand's ability reads "{T}, Pay 1 life, Sacrifice this land: Search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle." Activating it puts that ability on the stack (after you've already paid the cost, including sacrificing Flooded Strand). Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability, activated with X=2, targets that ability on the stack and creates 2 additional copies of it (per Gogo's own text: "Copy target activated or triggered ability you control X times"), and per [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6], this creates additional instances of the ability on the stack rather than granting anyone a new ability. That leaves 3 total instances of the Flooded Strand ability on the stack: the original plus 2 copies.

Under rule [707.10b], a copy of an ability copies all decisions made for it (including targets, if any) and, if the effect refers to objects used to pay its cost, it uses the objects used to pay the original's cost — so each copy still 'knows' Flooded Strand was the sacrificed land that paid for the ability, and copying an ability does not require paying its cost again. Each of the 3 instances independently resolves, searching your library for a Plains or Island card and putting it onto the battlefield, then shuffling (three separate searches and shuffles). Per [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9], the source of each copy is Flooded Strand itself, same as the original.

So Flooded Strand is sacrificed only once (as the original activation cost), but you end up putting 3 Plains/Island cards onto the battlefield, assuming your library has at least 3 legal cards to find each time.
